title: 03. Embeddings & Vector DBs: Vector DB Fundamentals — Collections, Namespaces, Distance Metrics
summary: A vector database is a specialized storage engine designed to store, index, and query dense numerical vectors at scale with sub-millisecond latency.

sections.title: ① Concept Explanation
sections.body:
A vector database is a specialized storage engine designed to store, index, and query dense numerical vectors at scale with sub-millisecond latency. Unlike traditional databases that retrieve records by exact key match or SQL filter, vector databases retrieve by approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search — finding vectors geometrically close to a query vector. Core concepts:
- **Collection/Index/Namespace**: The top-level container that holds vectors of a specific dimension with a configured distance metric. Equivalent to a table in SQL. Most DBs call it "collection" (Qdrant, Chroma, Milvus) or "index" (Pinecone) or "class" (Weaviate).
- **Point/Record**: A single vector with its ID, the embedding values, and a payload (JSON metadata).
- **Payload**: Arbitrary JSON metadata stored alongside each vector, used for metadata filtering.
- **Dimension**: The length of the stored vectors — must match the embedding model (e.g., 3072 for text-embedding-3-large).
- **Distance Metric**: The formula used to compute similarity between vectors.

diagrams.title: Inside a vector database query
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  Q["query vector + filter tenant=acme"] --> F{"metadata pre-filter"}
  F --> ANN["ANN index search — HNSW or IVF"]
  ANN --> TOP["top-k ids + distances"]
  TOP --> FETCH["fetch payload — text, source, page"]
  FETCH --> OUT(["results"])
diagrams.explain: A vector DB stores **vectors + payload + metadata** in collections. Queries combine an approximate nearest-neighbour search with **metadata filters** (tenant, date, permissions). Pick the distance metric your embedding model was trained for — usually cosine.

sections.title: ④ Visual Explanation
sections.body:
```
VECTOR DATABASE ARCHITECTURE
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

COLLECTION STRUCTURE:
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Collection: "rag_production" (COSINE, 1536d)
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Point {                                                  │
│   id: "chunk-001-abc",                                  │
│   vector: [0.12, -0.54, 0.89, ..., 0.33]  (1536 dims)  │
│   payload: {                                             │
│     "text": "Warranty covers defects for 2 years",      │
│     "source": "warranty_policy.pdf",                    │
│     "page": 4,                                          │
│     "tenant_id": "a3f8b29c",                           │
│     "created_at": "2026-01-15T10:30:00Z"               │
│   }                                                      │
│ }                                                        │
│ Point { id: "chunk-002-def", vector: [...], payload: {...} } │
│ ... (10,000,000 more points)                            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

HNSW INDEX LAYERS:
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 2 (coarse): ●────●────●  (few nodes, long-range links)
                  │
Layer 1 (medium): ●──●──●──●──●  (more nodes, medium links)
                  │
Layer 0 (fine):   ●─●─●─●─●─●─●─●─●  (all nodes, short links)

Query: finds approximate path through layers to nearest neighbor
       L2 → L1 → L0 → greedy search in L0 → top-K results

DISTANCE METRICS:
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Cosine:    1 - (v1·v2)/(|v1|·|v2|)  → angle between vectors
Euclidean: √Σ(v1[i]-v2[i])²          → geometric distance
Dot product: v1·v2                    → projection (magnitude matters)

For RAG with normalized embeddings:
  dot product = cosine (they're equivalent!)
  Use COSINE or DOT_PRODUCT (same result, different range)

VECTOR DB COMPARISON:
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DB         Hosted  Open-Source  Languages  Filter Mode    Best For
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Qdrant     ✓       ✓ (Rust)     REST/gRPC  Filtered HNSW  Production RAG
Pinecone   ✓       ✗            REST       Pre-filter     Managed cloud
Weaviate   ✓       ✓ (Go)       REST/gRPC  Filtered HNSW  Multi-modal
Chroma     ✗       ✓ (Python)   REST       Post-filter    Dev/prototyping
Milvus     ✓       ✓ (C++)      REST/gRPC  IVF/HNSW/PQ    Billion-scale
pgvector   ✗       ✓ (C)        SQL        Pre-filter     Existing Postgres
```

quiz.question: What are the three main vector distance metrics and which should you use for RAG?
options: Used when memory is the bottleneck — enables storing billions of vectors in RAM.
Exact (brute force): computes distance to every vector — O(n) per query, 100% recall.
IVF clusters vectors into Voronoi cells (via k-means), builds an inverted index of which vectors are in each cell, then at query time searches only the closest cells (nprobe parameter).
The three main metrics are: Cosine similarity (measures angle between vectors — ignores magnitude, focuses on direction), Euclidean distance (L2, measures geometric distance — sensitive…
quiz.explanation: The three main metrics are: Cosine similarity (measures angle between vectors — ignores magnitude, focuses on direction), Euclidean distance (L2, measures geometric distance — sensitive to magnitude), and Dot product (equivalent to cosine if vectors are normalized, otherwise magnitude-sensitive). For RAG with neural embedding models (OpenAI, BGE, Sentence Transformers): use cosine similarity.

quiz.question: How do namespaces/multi-tenancy work in vector databases, and why are they important?
options: Two approaches: pre-filtering (filter the candidate set before ANN search — can miss results if filter is too restrictive) and post-filtering (run ANN search, then apply…
Root Cause: HNSW graph grew too large for RAM, causing excessive disk I/O during graph traversal.
Qdrant stores HNSW graph in memory by default (fast, ~4 bytes/dim/vector).

Multi-tenancy allows one vector database cluster to serve multiple isolated tenants (users, teams, or datasets) without cross-contamination of results. Strategies: Separate collections per tenant (Qdrant, Chroma): Strong isolation, each tenant has own HNSW index. Higher memory overhead; Single collection + payload filter (Pinecone namespaces, Qdrant payload field): All vectors in one index, filtered by tenant_id at query…; Pinecone Namespaces: Purpose-built multi-tenancy — logical partitions within a single index, each with independent ANN search.
quiz.explanation: Multi-tenancy allows one vector database cluster to serve multiple isolated tenants (users, teams, or datasets) without cross-contamination of results. Strategies: Separate collections per tenant (Qdrant, Chroma): Strong isolation, each tenant has own HNSW index. Higher memory overhead.

quiz.question: What is HNSW and why is it the dominant ANN algorithm?
options: IVF clusters vectors into Voronoi cells (via k-means), builds an inverted index of which vectors are in each cell, then at query time searches only the closest cells (nprobe parameter).
Exact (brute force): computes distance to every vector — O(n) per query, 100% recall.
Used when memory is the bottleneck — enables storing billions of vectors in RAM.
HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a multi-layer graph where each layer is a navigation shortcut to lower layers.
quiz.explanation: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a multi-layer graph where each layer is a navigation shortcut to lower layers. Retrieval follows the shortcut layers to get close to the query, then fine-tunes in the bottom layer. It achieves O(log n) retrieval with 95-99% recall accuracy.

quiz.question: What is IVF (Inverted File Index) and when is it better than HNSW?
options: Used when memory is the bottleneck — enables storing billions of vectors in RAM.
Exact (brute force): computes distance to every vector — O(n) per query, 100% recall.
HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a multi-layer graph where each layer is a navigation shortcut to lower layers.
IVF clusters vectors into Voronoi cells (via k-means), builds an inverted index of which vectors are in each cell, then at query time searches only the closest cells (nprobe parameter).
quiz.explanation: IVF clusters vectors into Voronoi cells (via k-means), builds an inverted index of which vectors are in each cell, then at query time searches only the closest cells (nprobe parameter). Better than HNSW for massive datasets (>100M vectors) where HNSW graph memory becomes prohibitive. Tradeoff: lower recall than HNSW at same parameter settings.

quiz.question: What is Product Quantization and when is it used?
options: Exact (brute force): computes distance to every vector — O(n) per query, 100% recall.
HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a multi-layer graph where each layer is a navigation shortcut to lower layers.
IVF clusters vectors into Voronoi cells (via k-means), builds an inverted index of which vectors are in each cell, then at query time searches only the closest cells (nprobe parameter).
Used when memory is the bottleneck — enables storing billions of vectors in RAM.
quiz.explanation: PQ compresses vectors by splitting them into sub-vectors and approximating each with a codebook centroid. Reduces vector storage by 16-64x with minor recall degradation. Used when memory is the bottleneck — enables storing billions of vectors in RAM.
